tier_reason: Peer-reviewed CGO 2025 paper (abstract reproduced in the cage-meta README) reports a sandboxing speedup of over 5.1% from MTE-based bounds checks; a search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456 ties it to PolyBench/C on a Google Pixel 8 against plain wasm64. Not A because the artifact (Zenodo) and paper were unreachable, so benchmark code, flags and per-core setup could not be opened.

corrections.baseline: Plain 64-bit Wasm (wasm64/memory64) run in Wasmtime without MTE, where the sandbox relies on software bounds checks; the paper reports speedups 'over wasm64' (search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456; whether the baseline build is upstream Wasmtime or the fork with MTE off was not confirmed).
corrections.claimed_speedup: cage-meta README abstract: memory-safety runtime overhead <5.8% and memory overhead <5.3% (the BibTeX abstract on the same page says <3.7%), and MTE-based sandboxing 'achieving a speedup of over 5.1%'. Search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456 (snippet only): on a Google Pixel 8 (Tensor G3), PolyBench/C mean speedup of MTE sandboxing over wasm64 of 3.7±6.5%, 5.1±4.0% and 33.9±2.4% on the three core types (33.9% on the in-order Cortex-A510 cores); memory safety plus MTE sandboxing 2.1±5.6%, 4.5±4.1% and 29.2±2.5% versus wasm64.
corrections.workload: PolyBench/C kernels compiled to 64-bit Wasm with Cage's LLVM fork and run in the wasmtime-mte fork on a Google Pixel 8 (per search snippets of the paper); Cage offloads the wasm64 sandbox bounds check to Arm MTE and adds MTE heap/stack safety and PAC pointer protection.
corrections.hardware: Google Pixel 8 (Google Tensor G3) with Arm MTE and PAC, per the paper's artifact appendix as quoted in a search snippet; LLVM, wasmtime and benchmarks cross-compiled on an x86 host. Not confirmed from an opened page.
corrections.caveats: The CGO 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3696443.3708920, pp. 538-552), arXiv 2408.11456, the CGO slides on dse.in.tum.de and the Zenodo artifact (doi 10.5281/zenodo.13772996) were all unreachable here; per-core numbers come from search snippets only. The 5.1% is a mean with a ±4.0% spread on one core type; on the big cores the mean is 3.7% with a ±6.5% spread (spread larger than the mean), and only the in-order Cortex-A510 shows a large gain (33.9%). The win is against wasm64 software bounds checks, not against 32-bit Wasm with guard pages, which needs no explicit checks. Requires Arm MTE hardware (Pixel 8 class). README abstract (memory overhead <5.3%) and BibTeX abstract (<3.7%) disagree. wasmtime-mte is a research fork of bytecodealliance/wasmtime (12,557 commits, mostly upstream; last MTE commits 2026-01-14), not upstreamed; its README is the stock wasmtime README with no MTE instructions.

notes: Claim text in the record matches the cage-meta README exactly; hardware and per-core numbers added from search snippets of the arXiv version (marked snippet only). Keep at B; a paper-access retier could reach A if the Zenodo artifact names flags and harness. License is Apache-2.0 with LLVM exception (LICENSE file line 205).

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC 2023 paper whose abstract (search snippet only) reports up to 2.9x throughput-per-dollar versus Intel x86-64 cloud VMs; the public artifact (benchmarks/run_benchmarks_aws.py, make_figures.py, raw results in benchmarks/2022-12-22-20:09:12) runs the same Wasm on CPU via Wasmtime and natively. Not A: CPU models and Wasm build flags are not stated on opened pages and the paper itself could not be opened.

corrections.claimed_speedup: USENIX ATC 2023 abstract (search snippet only; usenix.org and the Princeton PDF were unreachable): throughput-per-dollar up to 2.9x compared with Intel x86-64 VMs in the cloud, for certain classes of compute-bound workloads, and in some cases matching the throughput-per-dollar of native CUDA baselines. No numbers on the repo pages opened; readme.md says the approach is 'less efficient than manual translation'.
corrections.baseline: Same Wasm modules on CPU with Wasmtime embedded in VectorVisor (--wasmtime=true) and native x86-64 Rust builds (cargo run --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu), on 4-vCPU AWS c5.xlarge (Intel) or c5a.xlarge (AMD) instances; hand-written CUDA versions (cuda-blockhash, cuda-blur) on the GPU for imagehash and imageblur.
corrections.hardware: GPU side: AWS g4dn.xlarge (1 NVIDIA T4, 4 vCPU), g5.xlarge (1 NVIDIA A10G, 4 vCPU) or g4ad.xlarge (AMD Radeon Pro V520); CPU baseline: AWS c5.xlarge (Intel) or c5a.xlarge (AMD); load generator c5a.8xlarge, all in us-east-1b (benchmarks/run_benchmarks_aws.py). Exact CPU models not named on the pages opened.
corrections.caveats: Headline metric is throughput per dollar of a GPU instance versus a 4-vCPU CPU instance, not raw throughput or latency, and the 2.9x applies only to some compute-bound workloads (search snippet of the abstract; paper at https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc23/presentation/ginzburg not reachable here). The repo holds figures (latency_throughput.png, latency_breakdown.png), make_figures.py and raw result directories (2022-12-22-20:09:12 is the paper's data per benchmarks/README.md) but no text summary of results. The Wasmtime CPU baseline is VectorVisor's embedded --wasmtime mode with a pinned wasmtime version, not the standalone CLI. readme.md admits it is less efficient than manual GPU translation; AMD V520 support is partial and sometimes crashes. benchmarks/README.md says the end-to-end evaluation takes about 24 hours on AWS. Last commit 2024-09-26 (stale).

notes: Record is accurate on metadata (Apache-2.0, 160 stars, last commit 2024-09-26, stale); baseline extended to the native x86 and CUDA rows the harness also runs. Only the abstract figure (2.9x throughput-per-dollar, snippet only) is available; a paper-access retier should extract per-benchmark ratios. Shortcoming: dollar-normalized metric, gains limited to compute-bound workloads.

tier_reason: First-party doc (Documentation/RegisterMachine.md) states a 7.4x CoreMark gain over WasmKit's own second-generation interpreter on an M1 Mac mini with a named Swift snapshot; the comparison with wasm3, stitch and wasmi is a chart without numbers and only claims 'well competitive'. The doc does not name its harness (Benchmarks/bench.py exists now but cannot be tied to the 2024 run), so C.

corrections.license: MIT (runtime modules); the GDBRemoteProtocol and WasmKitGDBHandler modules are Apache-2.0 with a Runtime Library Exception
corrections.compiler_and_flags: WasmKit built with swift build -c release, toolchain swift-DEVELOPMENT-SNAPSHOT-2024-09-17-a; CoreMark built with wasi-sdk clang 18.1.2 -O3 -D_WASI_EMULATED_PROCESS_CLOCKS (from the CoreMark log on the same page and Benchmarks/bench.py PORT_CFLAGS)
corrections.caveats: The headline 7.4x is against WasmKit's own older stack-based interpreter, not an external incumbent. Against wasm3, stitch and wasmi the doc only shows a chart (SVG with outlined glyphs, values not readable) and says 'well competitive', so no faster-than-incumbent claim exists. The second-generation CoreMark log on the same page shows WasmKit gen-2 at 291 iterations/s, wasmi at 1321 and wasmtime (JIT) at 11527; 7.4x of 291 is about 2155 iterations/s (derived from page data), still roughly 5x below wasmtime, and the log's machine and wasmi version are not stated, so a wasmi comparison cannot be derived. The doc says 'we have not done a comprehensive performance evaluation yet'. Single machine (2020 Mac mini M1), single CoreMark run, 2024-09 toolchain snapshot, so numbers are old for the 2026 code. A Benchmarks/bench.py harness (CoreMark, wasmi-benchmarks replay, wasm3/wasmi/wasmtime engines) exists in the repo but no results report.

notes: Accurate record; kept at C. Shortcoming: self-relative 7.4x only, no numeric win over wasm3/stitch/wasmi/wasmtime. An A case exists only for the self-relative claim (M1, Swift snapshot, -O3 CoreMark) but the harness used is unnamed. Metadata checked: 509 stars, last commit 2026-10-11, active.
